sourceCopy.name: Taylor Series Calculator
sourceCopy.title: Taylor Series Calculator Free | UsefulVerse
sourceCopy.description: Build a Taylor or Maclaurin polynomial, choose its center and order, and compare its value with the function. Free and local.
sourceCopy.intro: Choose an elementary function, expansion center, degree and evaluation point. Inspect each coefficient, the polynomial estimate and its pointwise error.
sourceCopy.howQuestion: What does a Taylor series calculator show?
sourceCopy.howAnswer: It builds a finite Taylor polynomial from derivatives at a chosen center. The reported error is the absolute difference at your selected point, not a guaranteed error bound over an interval.
sourceCopy.privacyAnswer: No. The polynomial and comparison are calculated in this browser; your values are not uploaded or saved.
howTo: Select one of the supported functions.
Enter the center, evaluation point and polynomial order.
Compare the Taylor approximation with the function value and review convergence notes.

example.label: Load example: eˣ about 0, order 2, at 1

fields.coefficientTable: Taylor polynomial terms in powers of (x − a)
fields.convergenceNote: For ln(x), √x and 1/x, the Taylor series has a finite convergence radius around the selected center. A polynomial can still be evaluated outside it, but may not approximate the function well.
fields.accuracyNote: Supported functions: eˣ, sin(x), cos(x), ln(x), 1/x and √x. Order 0–30; inputs are bounded to ±50. Trigonometric inputs use radians.
fields.formulaNote: Pointwise difference is |f(x) − Pₙ(x)|. It is not a maximum-error estimate or a formal remainder bound on a whole interval.

additionalFaqs.question: What is a Maclaurin polynomial?
additionalFaqs.answer: It is a Taylor polynomial centered at zero. This calculator lets you choose zero or another valid center.

additionalFaqs.question: Does the displayed difference guarantee accuracy throughout an interval?
additionalFaqs.answer: No. It is the absolute difference at your single evaluation point. A remainder bound across an interval requires additional derivative bounds and conditions.

additionalFaqs.question: Why can the polynomial be poor outside a convergence radius?
additionalFaqs.answer: The finite polynomial can be evaluated there, but the infinite Taylor series for logarithm, square root and reciprocal functions only converges inside its radius around the center.
